docs.text: terranode ¶ terranode helps organizations configure GIS field projects, send field teams out with a mobile app to collect data — points, lines, polygons, photos, video, and audio — and bring that data back into a shared map, even when the field has no signal. What you can do today ¶ Catalog management — import base maps, vector layers, and raster layers once, then reuse them across as many projects as you need, or build on a public catalog Terranode has already published. Project management — define a project's boundary, choose which catalog layers and surveys apply, and track progress from a dashboard. Survey collection — build custom forms field users fill out on mobile, with full support for offline capture and later sync. Organization-based access — every user belongs to one organization; project owners configure projects, field users collect data. Where to start ¶ New to terranode? Start with Getting started . Terms like catalog , project , and bundle are defined in the Glossary . Prefer the terminal? See Using the tn CLI . This is client-facing documentation Looking for internal architecture, runbooks, or API implementation notes instead? That lives in the separate engineering docs site.

docs.text: Using the tn command line ¶ tn is terranode's command-line client for working with organizations, catalogs, uploads, and data sources from a terminal or script. Early preview tn is new and not yet published anywhere you can pip install it from directly. Ask your terranode contact for access while that is being set up. Signing in ¶ tn auth login You'll be asked for your email and password. tn stores its own command-line token locally in ~/.config/tn/config.json so you don't have to log in again for every command. This is separate from your browser session in the web app. If you belong to more than one organization, pick a default organization ref: tn config set-org acme tn orgs list shows the organizations you belong to, including each organization's slug and id. tn auth whoami shows who you are and, for each organization, what you are allowed to do there. See Roles and permissions . Resource refs ¶ A ref is the value you type to identify something. For readable resources, a ref can be either the stable UUID id or the human-friendly slug shown in tn output. Refs accepted by tn today: Organization ref: organization id or slug. Catalog ref: catalog id or slug inside the selected organization. Data source ref: data source id or slug inside a catalog. Upload id: uploads are not named, so uploads stay id-only. API key id: API keys stay id-only. Slugs are easier to type, but they can be renamed. Use ids for long-lived scripts when stability matters. Working with catalogs ¶ tn catalogs list tn catalogs create --name "Field boundaries" --visibility private tn catalogs get field-boundaries tn catalogs update field-boundaries --name "New name" tn catalogs delete field-boundaries Add --json after tn to get machine-readable output instead of a table: tn --json catalogs list Uploading data into a catalog ¶ tn uploads create field-boundaries ./roads.geojson --wait This uploads the file and, with --wait , blocks until terranode has finished turning it into one or more data sources. Drop --wait to return immediately and check later: tn uploads list field-boundaries tn uploads get field-boundaries <upload-id> tn datasources list field-boundaries tn datasources get field-boundaries roads Data sources themselves aren't created or edited directly. They are created when an upload finishes processing. Managing your team ¶ Everyone can list the members of their organization. Everything else here needs the owner role. People are identified by email address. tn orgs members list tn orgs members set-role ana@example.com editor tn orgs members remove ana@example.com set-role takes owner , editor or field . remove takes the person out of the organization but keeps the record, and inviting the same address again brings them back. The organization always keeps at least one active owner, so changing or removing the last one is refused. To invite people, give one or more addresses and a role that applies to all of them: tn orgs invitations create ana@example.com bob@example.com --role field tn orgs invitations list tn orgs invitations resend ana@example.com tn orgs invitations revoke ana@example.com create prints one row per address. An address that can't be invited, such as someone who already belongs to the organization, doesn't stop the others, and the command exits with an error if any address failed. list shows invitations that are still open. An invitation that has expired is not listed: invite the same address again to renew it. Automating without your password ¶ If you want a script, CI pipeline, or server to use tn without your personal login, create an API key instead. You need to be an organization owner. tn orgs api-keys create --name "ci-pipeline" --role editor This mints a long-lived credential and, by default, switches this machine to use it. If the key is meant for somewhere else, add --mint-only : tn orgs api-keys create --name "ci-pipeline" --role editor --mint-only Wherever the key ends up, set it as TN_TOKEN in that environment: export TN_TOKEN = "<the key you were given>" export TN_ORG = "acme" List or revoke keys for your organization at any time: tn orgs api-keys list tn orgs api-keys revoke <key-id> See the Glossary for terms like catalog and organization used throughout this page.

docs.text: Getting started ¶ 1. Join or create your organization ¶ The first time you sign in, terranode asks for your organization's details. Every user belongs to exactly one organization — all of your catalogs, projects, and surveys live inside that boundary and stay private to it, with one exception: a catalog Terranode itself has published as public (see below). 2. Build (or import) a catalog ¶ Before you can configure a project, you need some GIS layers to work with — check the catalogs list for a public one from Terranode first; if there's one you can use as-is, you can skip straight to configuring a project with no import at all. Otherwise: Import vector or raster data from disk, or pull it from a cloud bucket you already have (S3, GCS, and similar). Assign a style to each layer so it renders consistently across projects. Tag and describe layers so your team can find them later — see Find anything below. 3. Configure a project ¶ Organization owners and editors can create and archive projects. Editing a project takes two things: a role that allows editing projects (all three roles do) and a part in that particular project, meaning you created it or you were assigned as its manager. Other owners and editors, and field members generally, can still see projects in their organization so they know what work is available to download and collect against. See Roles and permissions for the full picture. Project teams can assign organization members as managers, collectors, or reviewers. The person or API key that creates a project is always its first manager and cannot be removed from that role. Collector and reviewer roles will control more project-specific actions as those workflows are introduced. A project ties together: A boundary — the geographic area field work covers. A project can't start without one. A description and kind — enough context to explain the work and group it by your organization's local workflow. An estimated deadline and point goal — optional planning targets for the team. A review requirement — whether collected submissions need review before they are treated as final. Participating layers from your catalog — the base maps and reference data field users will see on their device. A project can include multiple layers, each using a catalog data source and style. Participating surveys — the forms field users fill out while collecting data. A project can include multiple surveys; start from a template when your organization has a reusable base or example form, then customize it for the project. 4. Send your team to the field ¶ Field users open the mobile app, sign in, and download the project. The download bundles the boundary, layers, and surveys so the app works with no network connection. As data comes back in, the project dashboard shows submission counts, survey breakdowns, and live tracking. Find anything ¶ The search bar at the top of terranode searches across catalogs, layers, projects, surveys, and users in your organization — one place to find anything, regardless of which "epic" it belongs to. See the Glossary for definitions of terms used throughout this documentation.

docs.text: Glossary ¶ Organization (org) : The tenant boundary in terranode. Every user belongs to exactly one organization. All catalog, project, and survey data is scoped to an organization, both at the application level and, as a defense-in-depth layer, via PostgreSQL Row-Level Security. terranode (the perennial org) : A built-in, always-present organization owned by the terranode team itself, used to publish a shared base catalog (base maps, reference layers) that other organizations can use without owning. Role : What a member is within an organization: owner , editor or field , shown in the web app as Gestor, Editor and Coletor. A person has one role in each organization they belong to, and an API key is minted with one. The role decides which permissions the member holds. Permission : One thing a role may do, named resource:action , such as catalog:write or project:update . The API enforces permissions on every request and reports the ones a credential holds, so the app and the tn CLI offer only what will work. Editing a particular project needs the project:update permission and a part in that project: its creator, or one of its managers. Catalog : The set of reusable GIS resources — layers, styles, raster and vector sources — that an organization curates. Catalog data is imported and exported, not hand-edited feature-by-feature, in the initial release. Layer : A single named GIS dataset (vector or raster) in a catalog, with an assigned style and metadata/tags. Layers are owned by exactly one catalog but may be referenced by many projects. Integration : An organization's connection to an external GIS platform — today ArcGIS Online or ArcGIS Enterprise. Data flows one way, into terranode: the user picks layers on the external side and they are pulled into catalogs. A catalog filled this way belongs to exactly one integration and does not accept manual uploads. Feature Service : The ArcGIS container that a terranode catalog maps to. Note that "feature dataset" and "feature class" are geodatabase concepts that publishing flattens away — the ArcGIS REST API exposes a portal item (the Feature Service) and the layers and tables inside it, nothing between them. Sync target : One remote layer or table an organization has subscribed to. It records where the data comes from on the external side and which catalog it lands in. Project : A configured field data collection effort: a boundary, a set of participating catalog layers, and a set of surveys. Projects use catalog data — they never own or duplicate it. Survey : A configurable form (similar in spirit to SurveyMonkey) that field users fill out on mobile devices while collecting GIS data — points, lines, polygons, and attached media (photos, video, audio). A survey can be created directly or from a survey template. Survey template : An organization-scoped reusable form definition. Creating a survey from a template copies the template schema into the survey. System survey template : A global template configured by terranode administrators and listed alongside organization-scoped templates. Bundle : The offline package a mobile client downloads before a field visit: the project's boundary, participating layers, and survey definitions, packaged so the field app can work with no network connectivity. Registered installation (device) : An app installation that has enrolled against a field seat, recorded so an organization can see which installations are exercising its seats and revoke one if needed. It is a record of a seat being exercised, not an inventory of hardware — one physical tablet shared by three crew members with their own accounts produces three registrations, since each is a separate person's seat. Row-Level Security (RLS) : A native PostgreSQL feature enforcing tenant isolation at the database layer, independent of application-level query filtering. Used here as a second, fail-closed layer beneath terranode's org-scoping.

docs.text: Google Sheets ¶ A tab of a Google Sheets spreadsheet can become a data source of points in a catalog. terranode reads it again on every sync, so edits in the sheet reach the map without exporting a CSV. Nothing is ever written back to the sheet. Only organization owners manage integrations. Connect a Google account ¶ Go to Integrações and add an integration with Google Sheets as its origin. Sign in with the Google account that has the spreadsheets, and approve. terranode asks for your email and for access to the files you choose in it, nothing else. The person who connects the account is the only one who can add spreadsheets from it, because adding one opens that account's Google Drive. Other owners see who that is on the integration's page. Add a tab ¶ On the integration's page, choose Adicionar planilha and pick the spreadsheet in Google's window. Shared drives are listed too. Choose a tab. A tab without latitude and longitude columns is listed but can't be chosen. Check the result. terranode proposes the coordinate columns from their names, and you can pick others. You see the column types, how many rows will be imported, and every row that can't be. Choose Adicionar aba . The spreadsheet becomes a catalog with its name, and the tab a data source named after the tab. The first sync starts right away. Renaming the tab in Google Sheets doesn't break anything: the next sync updates the same data source. What a tab needs ¶ A header in row 1. Every column with values needs a name, and two columns can't have the same name ( Nome and nome count as the same). Latitude and longitude columns. terranode recognizes them by name: Latitude , lat , Longitude , lon , long , lng , names that start or end with them ( Latitude (WGS84) , long_corrigida ), and x / y exactly. Decimal degrees. -23.55 , or -23,55 typed as text. Degrees, minutes and seconds ( 23°32'51"S ) aren't read. Latitude goes from -90 to 90, longitude from -180 to 180, and neither can be empty. One kind of value per column. A column of numbers with one n/a in it becomes a text column. Empty rows are skipped. Any other row with a bad coordinate stops the import. When a sync is blocked ¶ Every sync checks the tab before importing it. It stops, and changes nothing on the map, when: a column was removed or renamed, a column changed type (numbers that now hold text), a row has a missing or invalid coordinate. A new column doesn't block: it's imported, and from then on it's expected. Open Histórico de sincronizações in the tab's menu to see what happened. It lists the columns that changed, or the rows to fix with their row number in the sheet. Fix the sheet and sync again. If the change is on purpose, a renamed column for instance, choose Importar novamente como nova fonte instead. terranode checks the tab again and creates a new data source from its current columns. The old data source stays in the catalog with its data, style and project layers, marked as Desconectada , and isn't updated anymore. Sync on a schedule ¶ Choose Agendar sincronização in the tab's menu to sync it on its own: every hour, every day at a time, every week on a day at a time, or a custom cron expression in UTC. Times are in your browser's time zone. A schedule can't run more often than every 15 minutes, and a sync starts up to 15 minutes after its time. ArcGIS layers can be scheduled the same way. A scheduled sync first checks whether the spreadsheet changed. If it didn't, nothing is downloaded, and the history shows the check as Sem alterações na origem . Choosing sync by hand always downloads. A schedule pauses, and the tab shows Agendamento pausado with the reason, when a sync is blocked (see above), after five failed syncs in a row, or while the integration needs reconnecting. Fix the cause, then choose Retomar , or sync by hand: a sync that works resumes the schedule. Reconnecting the integration resumes its schedules by itself. If terranode can't open the spreadsheet ¶ terranode only reaches the spreadsheets picked in Google's window by the account that was connected. If the integration was reconnected with another Google account, or the file was removed from your Drive, syncs fail with a message asking you to pick the spreadsheet again. Pick it once more on the integration's page. Its tabs stay as they were. If the account removed terranode's access on Google's side, the integration shows an error. Reconnect it.

docs.text: Roles and permissions ¶ Everyone in an organization has one role, and the role decides what they can do there. The same rules apply in the web app, in the tn command line and in the API. The three roles ¶ Role Shown in the app as Who it is for Owner Gestor The people who run the organization: they manage the team, credentials and integrations, and can do everything an editor can. Editor Editor The people who set up the work: catalogs, forms and projects. Field Coletor The people who collect data in the field. The web app uses the names in the second column. The command line and the API use the names in the first: owner , editor and field . What each role can do ¶ Owner Editor Field See projects and the list of members Yes Yes Yes Create and archive projects Yes Yes No Edit a project See below See below See below Collect in the field with the app Yes Yes Yes Catalogs and data sources: view, upload, change Yes Yes No Forms and form templates: view Yes Yes Yes Forms and form templates: create and change Yes Yes No Integrations Yes No No Invite people, change roles, remove members Yes No No API keys and registered devices Yes No No Organization settings Yes No No Public catalogs are a Terranode-only capability ¶ Terranode's own organization can publish one of its catalogs as public, making it available for every other organization to browse and build project layers from — read-only, and without needing to import or own the data themselves. See Getting started for what that looks like day to day. No organization other than Terranode's own can publish a public catalog today, whatever role a member holds there — owner and editor included. Members of Terranode's own organization, whatever their role, also see a performance panel on a project's map page. It measures how the map loads raster layers and is meant for the Terranode team only. Editing a project takes two things ¶ Editing a project needs both of these: A role that allows editing projects. All three roles do. A part in that particular project. You created it, or you were assigned as one of its managers. Being an owner or an editor is not enough on its own. Another owner's project stays theirs to edit unless you were made one of its managers. The exception is a project that has no recorded creator, which any owner can edit. A field member who manages a project can edit it. They still cannot create or archive projects: managing one project does not make someone a project creator. The person or API key that creates a project is its first manager and cannot be removed from that role. API keys have a role too ¶ When an owner creates an API key, the key gets a role, and it can do what that role can do and nothing more. A key with the editor role, for example, can work with catalogs and forms but cannot create an integration. See what you can do ¶ tn auth whoami shows who you are, which organizations you belong to and, for each one, the list of things you are allowed to do there. It is the same list the web app uses to decide which sections to show you. Changing someone's role ¶ Owners can change a role from the members page in the web app, or with tn orgs members set-role . The change applies at once: the person's next request uses the new role, with no need to sign in again. An organization always keeps at least one active owner, so the last owner cannot be demoted or removed. See the Glossary for terms like organization and role .

docs.text: Importing from Survey123 ¶ A form built in Survey123 can become a terranode survey without typing its questions again. Upload the form's XLSForm spreadsheet and terranode creates the survey and opens it in the builder. Anything terranode can't represent is left out or simplified, and listed for you to review. Organization owners and editors can import surveys. Get the XLSForm ¶ Survey123 Connect: the form's folder has a .xlsx file with the form's name. That spreadsheet is the XLSForm. Survey123 website: open the form, then use Export to XLSForm from the form's menu. Only the form comes across. Responses already collected in Survey123 are not imported. Import ¶ On Formulários , choose Novo formulário and then Importar do Survey123 . Drop the .xlsx file, or choose Selecionar arquivo . It can be up to 5 MB. The new survey opens in the builder, named after the form's title (or the file's name if the form has no title). Above the fields, a summary says what didn't come across. Expand O que mudou na importação to see each item. The survey is already saved, and nobody has answered it yet, so any field can still be renamed, changed or removed. The summary isn't kept: once you dismiss it or leave the page, it doesn't come back. A file is refused, and no survey is created, when it isn't an .xlsx spreadsheet, has no survey sheet, has more than 2,000 rows on the survey sheet or 20,000 on the choices sheet, or has no question terranode can import. What comes across ¶ Survey123 question terranode field text Short text, or long text with the multiline appearance email Email integer , decimal , range Number select_one , select_multiple Choice, single or multiple, with the options of its list date , dateTime , time Date, Date and time, Time geopoint , geotrace , geoshape Geometry: point, line or polygon image Photos (one photo), or Signature with the signature appearance audio , barcode Audio, Barcode Also carried over: Labels , without their formatting. When the form has labels in several languages, Portuguese is used if there is one. Required questions marked yes . Choice options , using each choice's label. A select_one … or_other question accepts answers typed in by the person collecting. Number limits written as . >= 0 and . <= 300 . Defaults to the current date or time : today() or now() on a date question, and now() on a dateTime or time question. Display conditions ( relevant ) of these kinds, joined all by and or all by or : ${condicao} = 'ruim' on a single choice selected(${defeitos}, 'corrosao') on a multiple choice ${altura} > 10 , and = , >= , < , <= , on a number ${observacao} != '' , or string-length(${observacao}) > 0 : the question was answered A condition on a group applies to every question in it. What doesn't come across ¶ In Survey123 In terranode Repeats ( begin repeat ) and the questions in them Removed. Each one is listed as a removed section with its questions, at the top of the summary. Groups The questions stay, in order, without the group. note , calculate , hidden , file , rank , and metadata like start or username Removed select_one_from_file Short text Any other default value ( default ) Removed. The summary quotes it. A second location question Removed: a survey has one location Hints Removed Other display conditions, conditional required , other constraints Removed. The question is always shown, optional, and a number gets limits of −1,000,000,000 to 1,000,000,000. The summary quotes the original expression so you can redo it in the builder. Question names that aren't lowercase letters, digits and _ Adjusted, e.g. Número_Torre becomes numero_torre
